Musselburgh.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of East Lothian's Honest Toun
s1loc: Musselburgh, the Honest Toun on the Firth of Forth, anchors its visitor draw on Musselburgh Racecourse, which dates to 1816 and pulls over 70,000 racegoers a year across Sensational Racedays from the New Year meeting to Ladies Day and Oktoberfest. Alongside it sits Musselburgh Links, the Old Golf Course, played since 1672 and reckoned among the oldest courses in the world, with the River Esk and the Forth coast framing the town.

The leisure and activity layer runs along the shore at Levenhall Links and Fisherrow Sands, with Fisherrow Harbour berthing leisure boats and walkers picking up the John Muir Way as it passes the beach. Inland, Inveresk Lodge Garden, the canoe water of the Esk and the wider Brunton playing fields and parks keep operators busy through the warmer months and the school-holiday peaks.

Heritage and culture sit thick on the ground, from 16th-century Pinkie House and the Palladian Newhailes estate at the town's edge to the conservation village of Inveresk above the river. The Brunton Theatre and Halls form the cultural hub, hosting shows and events, while the annual Musselburgh Festival and the riding of the marches keep the Honest Toun's calendar full.

The visitor trade leans on Musselburgh's place at Edinburgh's doorstep, with frequent rail and bus links carrying day-trippers in minutes to the capital and out along the East Lothian coast to Prestonpans and Aberlady. A spread of guest houses, inns and seafront accommodation serves racegoers and golfers, with the surrounding beaches, golf links and the Forth shoreline driving a strong seasonal flow.

Penzance.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of West Cornwall
s1loc: Penzance closes the far western coast of Cornwall around Mount's Bay, with the art deco Jubilee Pool - the UK's largest seawater lido and home to a geothermal pool - sitting on the seafront below the town. The tidal castle island of St Michael's Mount, cared for by the National Trust, crowns the bay just along the shore at Marazion, while the Penzance Promenade and harbour give the resort its long-running summer pull.

The leisure and activity layer ranges from Morrab Gardens, a subtropical three-acre Victorian garden of palms and tree ferns, to Penlee Park and the open coast path running out to the fishing villages of Newlyn and Mousehole. Watersports and coasteering off Mount's Bay, the South West Coast Path and day boats from the harbour keep activity operators working through the season's long Cornish daylight.

Heritage and culture run deep here, from Penlee House Gallery and Museum, the only public gallery devoted to the Newlyn School painters, to the granite Egyptian House and the historic Chapel Street quarter. The town's Golowan Festival and Mazey Day, the Acorn arts venue and nearby Newlyn Art Gallery give Penzance a busy events calendar through the warmer months.

The visitor trade is built on Penzance being the gateway to the Isles of Scilly, with the Scillonian III ferry sailing from the harbour and Skybus flights from Land's End Airport just out of town. Penzance railway station sits beside the quay as the end of the line from London Paddington, and a deep base of hotels, guest houses and the surrounding draws of Land's End and St Ives feed a strong seasonal flow.

Melksham.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of west Wiltshire
s1loc: Melksham sits on the River Avon in west Wiltshire, a Domesday market town whose 19th-century life as a small spa rival to Bath left the surviving crescent of Lodging Houses and a Pump Room at the Spa. The historic core gathers around St Michael and All Angels Church, Canon Square and Church Walk, with the Melksham Heritage Discovery Trail guiding visitors through the old streets and along the riverside.

The leisure and activity layer centres on King George V Park - known locally as The Park - with its riverside playing fields, playground, canoe club on the Avon and summer splash pad, while Conigre Mead Nature Reserve offers quieter wildlife walks beside the water. The Kennet and Avon Canal threads through the edge of town, drawing boaters, cyclists and towpath walkers across the warmer months.

Heritage and culture spread out from the town into a countryside thick with draws, from the National Trust's Lacock Abbey and the Fox Talbot Museum in nearby Lacock to the medieval village streets that double as a familiar film location. The Avon Valley, the events at The Park and the surrounding Wiltshire downs give Melksham a steady local calendar of fairs, markets and seasonal gatherings.

The visitor trade leans on Melksham's position between Bath, Chippenham and Trowbridge, with the railway station reopened on the TransWilts line and good road links along the A350 carrying day-trippers in and out. Inns, guest houses and the trade serving canal and walking visitors underpin the base, with Bath's world heritage city, Lacock and the wider Wiltshire countryside driving the seasonal day-trip draw.

Seaham.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Durham coast
s1loc: Seaham anchors County Durham's Heritage Coast around its harbour, where Ray Lonsdale's corten-steel Tommy statue - the weary First World War soldier at 11:01am on Armistice morning - has become the town's landmark on the seafront. The harbour and Seaham Marina, the county's only marina, draw visitors to the quayside, with the North Sea cliffs and the Durham Coastal Footpath framing the town.

The leisure and activity layer is led by the famous sea glass, the tumbled and frosted fragments from the old Londonderry Bottle Works that wash up across Seaham Hall Beach and draw beachcombers year round. Boat trips and angling run from the harbour, while the wider coast at Nose's Point, Blast Beach and the walks toward Dawdon and Dalton-le-Dale give activity operators a busy summer.

Heritage and culture reach back to Seaham Hall, where Lord Byron married Annabella Milbanke in 1815 - parents of Ada Lovelace - now a luxury coastal hotel, and to the Norman St Mary the Virgin church above the shore. The ruins of 16th-century Dalden Tower, the town's mining and bottle-works history and a calendar of harbour-side events round out a distinctive coastal heritage offer.

The visitor trade leans on Seaham's place between Sunderland and the Durham coast, with the railway station and the A19 carrying day-trippers in from across the North East. Seaham Hall and a spread of seafront hotels, guest houses and harbour-side trade serve the visitors, while the sea glass, the beaches and the nearby draws of Sunderland and the Durham coast drive a strong seasonal flow.

Horwich.region: Horwich and the West Pennine Moors
Horwich.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the West Pennine Moors
s1loc: Horwich sits beneath the West Pennine Moors on the edge of Bolton, with Rivington Pike and its 18th-century Pike Tower dominating the skyline above the town and drawing walkers up the slopes of Winter Hill. The moorland, the Anglezarke and Yarrow reservoirs and the open hills give Horwich a big outdoor visitor draw, while the Middlebrook complex and the Toughsheet Community Stadium anchor the modern leisure and events end of town.

The leisure and activity layer runs through Lever Park, gifted by Sir William Lever, and the celebrated Rivington Terraced Gardens climbing the hillside past the Pigeon Tower and Japanese Gardens toward the Pike. Rivington Hall Barn, the replica Liverpool Castle by Rivington Reservoir, mountain-bike trails on Lever Park and the climb to Winter Hill's trig point keep walkers, cyclists and family visitors busy across the year.

Heritage and culture trace back to Horwich's Loco Works railway past, with the parish church of Holy Trinity, the old town centre and the wider Rivington estate carrying the area's story. Lord Leverhulme's gardens, the historic barns at Rivington and Anderton, and the events and concerts staged at the stadium and Middlebrook give the town a busy seasonal calendar across the warmer months.

The visitor trade leans on Horwich's place beside the M61 and Bolton, with Horwich Parkway station and frequent links carrying day-trippers out to Rivington and the West Pennine Moors. Hotels and lodges around Middlebrook, the retail and leisure draw of the complex and the trade serving moorland walkers underpin the base, with Rivington, Winter Hill, Adlington and the nearby Chorley countryside driving a strong seasonal flow.

Hailsham.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Sussex Weald
s1loc: Hailsham anchors the Wealden country of East Sussex, with the moated Tudor house and medieval gatehouse of Michelham Priory - founded by the Augustinians in 1229 and ringed by England's largest medieval moat - the marquee draw just outside town at Upper Dicker. The town's market history, St Mary's parish church and the rolling countryside between the South Downs and the High Weald frame its visitor appeal.

The leisure and activity layer is led by Knockhatch Adventure Park, with its playground, animal collection of meerkats, owls and capybara and seasonal attractions, alongside the Cuckoo Trail, the 14-mile walking and cycling path along the old railway between Heathfield and Polegate. The watermill and Bronze Age roundhouse at Michelham and the wider Wealden lanes give activity operators a busy season.

Heritage and culture run from the restored Hailsham Pavilion cinema and theatre on George Street to the town's old rope-making and market past, with Michelham Priory's gardens, sculptures and watermill run by the Sussex Archaeological Society. The events calendar, the country shows and the markets, plus nearby Herstmonceux Castle and the Observatory Science Centre, give the area a rich seasonal programme.

The visitor trade leans on Hailsham's place inland from the coast, an easy hop from Eastbourne, Bexhill and the wider 1066 Country, with road links along the A22 and A27 and Polegate station carrying day-trippers in. Inns, guest houses and the trade serving Cuckoo Trail walkers and Michelham visitors underpin the base, while the South Downs, the Pevensey Levels, Arlington Reservoir and the East Sussex coast drive a strong seasonal draw.

Chesham.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Chilterns
s1loc: Chesham is a historic market town in the Chess Valley and a gateway to the Chilterns National Landscape, with the 12th-century St Mary's Church and its medieval interior anchoring the old town. Lowndes Park, gifted to the town in 1953 and home to the Bronze Age Rolling Pin burial mound, spreads above the centre, while the timber-framed streets carry the town's long-running market and visitor draw.

The leisure and activity layer runs along the River Chess, with Chesham Moor and its pool and tennis courts, the riverside paths past the old Lord's Mill, and the celebrated Chess Valley Walk threading ten miles down to Rickmansworth past Latimer and Chenies. The surrounding Chiltern beech woods, the hills and the Tudor Chenies Manor give walkers and family visitors a busy year-round draw.

Heritage and culture trace the town's famous four Bs - beer, boots, brushes and Baptists - through Chesham Museum and the 16th and 17th-century timber-framed buildings of the Old Town and High Street. Self-guided trails, the town's market heritage and the events calendar in Lowndes Park and the old centre keep Chesham's cultural offer lively across the seasons.

The visitor trade leans on Chesham being the furthest stop on the London Underground, with the Metropolitan line running direct via Baker Street and carrying day-trippers out to the Chilterns hills. Inns, guest houses and the trade serving walkers on the Chess Valley Walk underpin the base, while Amersham, Chenies Manor and the wider Chiltern countryside drive a strong seasonal day-trip draw.
